What makes this AI?+

A Gaussian-process learning model predicts energy and temperature from the completed experiments. After every result it is fitted again. Expected improvement, weighted by predicted temperature feasibility, chooses the next untested design. Predictions and their uncertainty are saved before that design is simulated.

This is Bayesian optimization, an established machine-learning method. It is not a language model, a scripted list of winning designs, or a new optimization algorithm. Uncertainty describes the learning model; it is not a calibrated error bar for real hardware.

Gaussian-process Bayesian optimization, Snoek et al. ↗
Constrained Bayesian optimization, Gelbart et al. ↗
Fair comparison & reproducibility+

The joint AI and random search get the same four initial experiments and the same total budget. Placement-only AI gets the same budget but keeps backup settings fixed. All winners are chosen using training results. Only then are they evaluated on longer, different fault conditions.

One design trial tests three training faults for 600 seconds each. A budget of 18 therefore means 54 training simulations per search, with duplicate shared observations cached. Every design uses six tiles and the same scenario set. The AI lab has unequal server loads, temperature-triggered backup, varied heat-transfer conductances, and flow-dependent pump costs. The manual illustration uses three equal loads and a fixed backup cost; it is a separate teaching setup.

The held-out suite is fixed and visible in the source for reproducibility, but its results are never given to the optimizer. It is not an externally administered blind test. Simulation gains do not establish gains on real hardware.

What’s the research gap? What did Valency find?+

Our question: can a small experiment budget find a recovery design that survives unfamiliar cooling failures?

The candidate contribution is the joint placement-and-backup fault benchmark, its learning loop, and the resulting reproducible evidence. AI thermoelectric optimization, heat harvesting, Bayesian optimization, and counting cooling costs all have prior work.

OPEN THE NOTEBOOK

Real equations.
Visible assumptions.

The mechanism is established. This particular rack, its temperatures, and its performance are simulated and have not been validated against hardware.

01 How the electricity is calculated+

A difference in temperature makes voltage.

Voc = α (Th − Tc)

α is the module’s Seebeck coefficient. Th and Tc are the hot and cold face temperatures.

I = Voc / (R + RL)
P = I² RL

Each tile has a matched electrical load, RL = R. This idealizes maximum-power operation at the current face temperatures. Conversion electronics are not modeled.

The generator also conducts heat.

Q̇h = α ThI − ½ I²R + KΔT
Q̇c = Q̇h − P

Heat entering the tile equals heat leaving plus generated electricity. K is thermal conductance; the αTI terms use kelvin. Tiles are thermally parallel, with independent matched loads.

Source: Ferrotec, Power Generation §13 ↗
02 What blocking a pipe actually changes+

Water carries energy away.

Q̇flow = ṁ cp (Twater − Tsupply)

Closing a valve sets that branch’s mass flow ṁ to zero. The water already in the branch stays there, stores heat, and can warm up. The other branches keep their assumed regulated flow.

Source: Bosch, water heat output ↗

Temperatures respond over time.

C dT/dt = Q̇in − Q̇out
Q̇conduction = G (T₁ − T₂)

Each branch has one hot-plate, cold-plate, and water temperature. Their finite heat capacities prevent instant jumps. A parallel conduction path and passive heat loss remain when water stops. The model resolves neither fluid turbulence nor internal CPU hotspots. In the manual illustration, backup is an assumed independent path supplying half flow with a fixed electrical cost. The AI lab instead learns a temperature trigger and flow setting, with a calculated flow-dependent pump cost described below.

Source: MIT thermodynamics notes §6.7.2 ↗
03 Manual illustration: parameters & limitations+

This table belongs to the manual illustration. The AI lab’s parameters and objective are in section 04 below. These are representative teaching parameters, not measurements from your rack. All-open equilibrium is calculated before the clock starts.

Module properties are independent synthetic assumptions: α = 0.05 V/K, R = 2.5 Ω and K = 0.6 W/K, held constant. No manufacturer coefficient dataset is distributed. Real properties vary with temperature. Our fixed heat capacities and conductances are simplifications; the 25°C supply is an imposed boundary whose cooling energy is outside this model.

Background: temperature-dependent module modeling §11 (not the source of our assumed values) ↗

There is no measured calibration, uncertainty distribution, pump curve, full hydraulic network, or physical safety validation. Blocking a pipe does not guarantee an immediate fall in power: both face temperatures change, and power follows their difference. The manual illustration makes no novelty claim. The AI benchmark’s narrower candidate contribution is described in its research-gap section; real-world improvement is not established.

Read the simulation source ↗

04 AI lab: objective, pumping cost & test protocol+

Recover electricity without crossing the temperature limit.

Enet = ∫ [Σ Ptiles − 0.90 W − Pbackup] dt
Score = minscenarios Enet
Constraint: max Thot plate ≤ 80°C

The optimizer maximizes the worst scenario’s net recovery. The 80°C limit is an illustrative benchmark rule, not a certified hardware rating. Normal cooling draws another assumed 3 W, excluded from this incremental balance. Chillers, conversion losses and pump heat in the coolant are outside this model.

The training set uses server heat loads of 240 / 200 / 160 W, a 25°C supply and room, and a complete blockage in A, B or C at 30 seconds. Each design starts at its own all-open equilibrium. The score includes 600 seconds; preparation energy is excluded.

Six held-out tests run for 900 seconds and vary partial blockage, supply/room temperature, load distribution, main flow and heat-transfer conductances. Fault onset stays at 30 seconds. Their results cannot influence the search.

More backup water costs more electricity.

Pbackup = Δp ṁ / (ρ η)
Δp = 25,000 Pa × [ṁ / (0.005 kg/s)]²

The first relation is hydraulic power divided by assumed overall efficiency. The quadratic pressure-flow relation is an assumed resistance model, not a measured pump curve. We assume water density 997 kg/m³ and efficiency 25%.

Each branch can add 25%, 50%, 75% or 100% of the normal 0.01 kg/s flow. That costs about 0.063 / 0.502 / 1.69 / 4.01 W per active branch. Backup turns on at 66, 70, 74 or 78°C and off 2°C lower. The controller checks temperatures every second; it receives no fault-location signal.

The AI and manual models share the same constant-property thermoelectric equations, heat capacities, and nominal conductances. All example design values remain uncalibrated.

05 What has actually been demonstrated before?+

Heat-to-electricity in data centers is established research.

The H2P researchers built a hardware prototype to harvest warm-water data-center heat with thermoelectric generators. Their measurements investigated water temperature, flow rate, and CPU utilization. This supports the basic feasibility of the mechanism. It does not validate our example parameters, blocked-pipe experiment, or predictions.

Read the original H2P paper (PDF) ↗

Optimizing thermoelectric arrays under uneven temperatures also has prior work. Our optional layout comparison is a transparent model experiment, not proof of an original invention.

Read the 2022 array-reconfiguration study ↗
